newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - BROKERS. CATASTROPHES..

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Marsh McLennan's second quarter results give the impression its bold acquisition of Johnson & Higgins has so far gone smoothly. As well as a healthy 26 per cent increase in overall income, profits from non-life business were up 17.5 per cent. While this is 0.9 per cent down on last year, it is no mean achievement in a soft market where broker costs are being pared to the bone.

Usually in such a large acquisition you initially lose more than you gain, and the second quarter is traditionally weaker anyway. As one analyst commented, if there was ever a quarter where you could have expected a negative surprise, this was it.

One would expect business margins to improve when the effect of the technological investments made by both operations kicks in. In addition the top management is all now in place and cost cutting measures under way.
If were any hidden traps in the acquisition, Marsh Mac does not seem to have fallen into them yet.
--oo0oo--

The first six months of 1997 have produced no major catastrophes - much to the relief of catastrophe insurers nervous in the knowledge they have been allowing their rates to get very low. Continued devastating floods in Central Europe have served as a reminder that the situation can change quickly.

The reinsurance market will be impacted by these events, although the degree will depend on how claims are presented. Most contracts will have the standard hours clause wording for flood which allows an aggregation of 168 hours to form one occurrence. This cover is reinstatable for a further 18 hours depending on when actual flood losses are deemed to have happened.

Levels of flood insurance cover vary between the countries - it is given free in Czech householders policies but limited on commercial policies. In Germany flood cover is sold separately for households but included on standard motor policies.

Over the weekend Hurricane Danny hit Alabama, causing President Clinton to declare parts of the state disaster areas, while the powerful Typhoon Rosie took five lives and brought havoc to the transportation system when it hit Japan.

Several meteorological experts, including veteran weather-watcher professor Bill Gray of Colorado State University predict this year's hurricane season will be marked by greater than average activity.

Using forecast equations that are developed from 47 years of historical data, Bill Gray's team says that there will be 11 named storms this year (against an average of 9.3) with at least three intense hurricanes in store.
With world catastrophe insurance rates at probably less than 50 per cent of their peak in 1994/95, many underwriters will not rest easy until the season is over.
